clue.text: The early break can be tough

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it up, so the letters of the two words are scattered and reassembled

explanation.surface: Getting up at dawn to snap someone's sleep can be a hard thing to bear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' is the anagram signal, applied to THE and EARLY together; 'can be' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat that is chewy and hard to cut is described as like hide, which is what the adjective conveys.

clue.text: Start the midday meal about one

indicators.note: about here means going round, so the meal surrounds the single letter

parts.note: lunch is the meal eaten at midday
a means one, as in a single item

explanation.surface: Begin eating lunch at around one o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts A (one) inside LUNCH. 'about one' reads like a time of day, which is the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: To launch a project is to set it going or begin it.

clue.text: Inattentive scholar shown up and told to go

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top, so reversed

parts.note: a BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a graduate scholar
sent means told to go somewhere, dispatched

explanation.surface: A daydreaming student is exposed and dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shown up' reverses BA (Bachelor of Arts) to AB in this down entry, then SENT follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone absent-minded is not paying attention, their thoughts elsewhere.

clue.text: Earth's turbulent interior

indicators.note: turbulent describes violent disturbance, so the letters of the planet's name are churned up

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: The core of our planet is a churning mass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turbulent' rearranges EARTH; the possessive 's adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The core of something, its centre, is its inner part.

clue.text: Gunmen hint it's a continual struggle to attain success

definitions.text: a continual struggle to attain success

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the British Army's gunners
a trace is a hint or slight suggestion

explanation.surface: Armed men hinting that life is a constant battle to get ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: RA (Royal Artillery) are gunmen in crossword terms, not criminals; 'it's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes the fiercely competitive pursuit of wealth or status in modern working life.

clue.text: Neat beasts

explanation.surface: Tidy animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' is an old word for oxen and cows, still seen in 'neatherd' and 'neat's-foot oil'; it is not the adjective meaning tidy.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat is an archaic collective term for bovine livestock, and beasts is the farmer's general word for the same herd animals.

clue.text: Such a downfall may be totally overwhelming

definitions.text: Such a downfall may be totally overwhelming

parts.words: Such a downfall may be totally overwhelming
parts.note: downfall reads like a ruin, but it is meant literally: a mass falling down a mountainside that buries everything

explanation.definitionFit: A huge slide of snow down a slope is a literal downfall, and it smothers whatever lies in its path.

clue.text: Scullion goes to hell

parts.note: turns means goes, as in it is your turn or one goes next
the pit is a name for hell

explanation.surface: A kitchen servant is condemned to perdition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link between the two pieces. A scullion was a lowly kitchen servant; this one turned the roasting spit.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically, a kitchen boy employed to rotate meat over the fire was a menial kitchen hand of that kind.

clue.text: Stop with some exasperation when put in jeopardy

parts.note: to end is to stop
anger is a measure of exasperation

explanation.surface: Losing your temper and halting puts you at risk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' and 'when' are links joining the pieces and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To imperil something is to expose it to harm or risk.

clue.text: The newly-rich sup possibly on pastries

indicators.note: possibly signals that the word sup could be arranged differently, as one possible rearrangement

parts.note: tarts are pastries with a filling

explanation.surface: The nouveaux riches may dine on fancy cakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' turns SUP into UPS; 'on' simply places that before TARTS in this across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Upstarts are people who have suddenly risen in wealth or status and behave with arrogance, much like parvenus.

clue.text: Put in braces

parts.note: a brace is a couple, as in a brace of pheasants, so to put things in braces is to group them in twos rather than to fit dental wire

explanation.definitionFit: A brace means a set of two, so arranging items in braces means matching them up in couples.

clue.text: A woman held in a case of mistaken identity

indicators.note: held in says the woman's name is gripped inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A lady is detained after being mistaken for someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held in' points into 'mistaken identity', where the letters bridge the two words; 'a case of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a female forename, as in the children's author Blyton.

clue.text: Limit studies with tutor

parts.note: to con is an old verb meaning to study or learn by heart
to train someone is to tutor or coach them

explanation.surface: A student restricts their reading by working with a private teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: CON for study is an old word kept alive in crosswords; 'with' just joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To restrict something is to hold it within bounds, which is what both verbs mean.

clue.text: Painter turning on a boy for lighting up

indicators.note: turning means the letters for the painter are flipped round to run backwards

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: An artist rounds on a lad caught striking matches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses RA (a Royal Academician) to AR, which goes on top of SON; 'a' and 'for' are links. 'lighting up' is meant to sound like smoking, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberately setting fire to property is a crime, so 'lighting up' a building is a jocular description of it.

clue.text: Nothing more than water

explanation.surface: Just a drop of H2O.
explanation.walkthrough: A small lake or pond is called a mere in British place names, such as Windermere.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means only or simply; as a noun it is a lake or pond, a body of water.

clue.text: Schedule can include an article to keep in mind

parts.note: to enter something is to record or list it, as on a schedule

indicators.note: include means one piece takes the other within it

parts.note: a tin is a can
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A timetable might have room for one item worth remembering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'include' puts A inside TIN, which follows ENTER; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To harbour a thought or consider an idea is to hold it, as in entertaining doubts.

clue.text: Waste-refuse

explanation.surface: Rubbish and garbage, read as one compound.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen makes the clue look like a pair of nouns for rubbish, but both halves are verbs here.
explanation.definitionFit: To waste away is to deteriorate or fade, and to refuse an offer is to turn it down politely; the verb covers both senses.

clue.text: City man taking ship after the end of September

indicators.note: the end of here means only the closing part of the month's name is kept, cutting away its front

parts.note: a liner is a large passenger ship

explanation.surface: A townsman boards a cruise ship once September is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the end of September' is its last three letters, BER; 'taking' and 'after' are links placing LINER behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A native or inhabitant of Germany's capital is called this, so he is a man from that city.

clue.text: Old entertainer, married this month — about fifty

parts.note: inst., short for instant, means of this month in old business letters
re means about or concerning
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A performer from the past got wed this month at around fifty.
explanation.walkthrough: INST (instant) is old commercial shorthand for 'this month', as in 'your letter of the 5th inst.'
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval travelling singer or poet was a performer at court, an entertainer of former times.

clue.text: Spite may be shown by the French in communication

indicators.note: the clue says the letters of the word spite may be shown in another order, which flags a rearrangement

parts.note: le is the French word for the

explanation.surface: Malice can be displayed by the French in a message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be shown' rearranges SPITE into EPIST, and LE (French for 'the') follows; 'by' and 'in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal letter, especially one in the New Testament, is a piece of written correspondence sent to someone.

clue.text: Wild seer giving tongue

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters of the prophet's word run riot

explanation.surface: A frenzied prophet speaking in tongues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' rearranges SEER; 'giving' is a link. This is the old name for the Gaelic language.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Gaelic language of Scotland or Ireland, and a tongue is a language.

clue.text: Restrain a supporter

explanation.surface: Hold back a fan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a supporter' sounds like a football fan, but it is the stalk that holds up a flower or leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem a flow is to check it, and a plant's stalk is what holds up its flower or leaf.

clue.text: Reservation of the boards without an alternative

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside means the word for theatre goes round the other

parts.note: the boards is a name for the stage, the theatre
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Booking seats at the theatre with no other option.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here, not lacking: STAGE goes round OR. 'an' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping something in reserve, held back for later use, is keeping it stored.

clue.text: It goes badly for the self-centred individual

indicators.note: badly suggests the letters of the two words have gone wrong and are jumbled

explanation.surface: Things turn out poorly for the selfish person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges IT GOES; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A person preoccupied with their own interests is wrapped up in self.

clue.text: A good man having seen much of life gets put on

parts.note: St, short for saint, stands for a good man
someone aged has lived a long time and seen a great deal

explanation.surface: A virtuous person with long experience is exploited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' looks like 'deceived' but means presented, as a play is; 'A' and 'gets' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A play is mounted or produced in a theatre, so to be put on means to be presented.

clue.text: Beam about Sarah's comeback

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the whole string of letters is taken back the other way

parts.note: re means about or concerning
Sal is a short form of the name Sarah

explanation.surface: A beam of light greets Sarah as she returns to the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comeback' turns RE plus SAL (a pet form of Sarah) backwards as one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser produces a narrow, intense ray of coherent light, so beam describes its output.

clue.text: If the head's held in disrespect that's a danger signal

indicators.note: held in tells us one word is enclosed within the other, gripped inside it

parts.note: a slight is an insult or act of disrespect
the top is the head of something

explanation.surface: A leader regarded with contempt is a sign that trouble lies ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held in' puts TOP inside SLIGHT; 'If the' and 'that's a' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A red traffic signal warns drivers to halt, so it is a warning of hazard ahead.

clue.text: Superior port

explanation.surface: A better harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: Liège is a Belgian city on the Meuse with a major river port; the accent is dropped in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A feudal lord to whom service was owed was one's superior, and the Belgian city is a river port.

clue.text: No right course for this country

parts.note: a way is a course or route

explanation.surface: A nation where no proper path is available.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' just links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Scandinavian kingdom, a nation on the western side of the peninsula.

clue.text: Providing work

explanation.surface: Supplying a job.
explanation.walkthrough: Catering for someone is providing for them; catering is also the trade of supplying food, a line of work.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb sense is supplying what is needed, and the noun sense is the business of preparing meals for events, an occupation.

clue.text: Arnold's changed his name

indicators.note: changed indicates that the letters of the man's name are altered into a new order

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A man called Arnold has had his name changed by deed poll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges ARNOLD; the possessive 's adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a man's forename, famous from the medieval French epic about Charlemagne's paladin.

clue.text: Didn't like taking action about check-up

indicators.note: about means one word surrounds the other, going round it

parts.note: a deed is an action
a test is a check-up or examination

explanation.surface: Someone disliked having to undergo a medical examination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' places DEED round TEST; 'taking' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe something is to hate it intensely, a strong form of disliking.
